title: How to Identify the Right Pattern

sections.heading: Why Pattern Recognition Matters
sections.content: Most DSA problems are variations of a small set of patterns. Instead of memorizing hundreds of solutions, learn to read a problem, spot its clues, and map it to a pattern. This topic is your decision guide for the whole course. Come back to it whenever you are stuck.

sections.heading: The 5-Step Approach to Any Problem
items: 1. Read the input type: array, string, linked list, tree, graph, grid, or numbers
2. Read the goal: find, count, maximize, minimize, check existence, or list all
3. Read the constraints: n decides the target time complexity
4. Match the clues to a pattern using the tables in this topic
5. Start from brute force, then optimize with the pattern

sections.heading: Decision Flow: Arrays and Strings
sections.content: Ask in this order. Is the array sorted? Try Two Pointers or Binary Search. Is the question about a contiguous range? Try Sliding Window or Prefix Sum. Do you need fast lookups or counts? Use a HashMap. Are values within 1 to n? Try Cyclic Sort. If none fit, sort first and see what changes.

sections.heading: Decision Flow: Trees and Graphs
sections.content: Is it a tree? Use DFS for properties of paths or subtrees and BFS for levels. Is it a graph? Use BFS for shortest path with equal weights, Dijkstra for weights, Topological Sort for dependencies, and Union Find for connectivity. A grid is a graph where each cell connects to its 4 or 8 neighbors.

sections.heading: Decision Flow: Optimization Problems
sections.content: If you must find the best answer, ask whether a local choice is always safe. If yes, try Greedy. If the choices overlap in subproblems, use DP. If the answer itself can be guessed and verified quickly, use Binary Search on Answer. If you must list every solution, use Backtracking.

sections.heading: Brute Force First, Then Optimize

rows.difference: Window tracks a contiguous range and its contents; two pointers often move from opposite ends
Window needs all positives or a monotonic condition; prefix sum + map handles negatives
BFS gives the shortest path in unweighted graphs; DFS is simpler for exploring everything
Greedy never reconsiders a choice; DP tries all choices and reuses results
Backtracking lists all answers; DP counts or optimizes when subproblems repeat
Heap is better for top K on large or streaming data; sorting is simpler for one-time results
BFS needs equal edge weights; Dijkstra handles non-negative weights

sections.heading: When You Are Stuck
items: Write a brute force solution and find the repeated work
Sort the input and see if the problem becomes easier
Try a HashMap or HashSet to remove an inner loop
Draw a small example by hand and trace what you do
Ask if the problem has overlapping subproblems (DP) or a monotonic answer (Binary Search)
Think about the problem in reverse
Try small inputs (n = 0, 1, 2) to find the base cases

sections.heading: Interview Communication Tips
items: Restate the problem and confirm the input and output
Ask about constraints, duplicates, negatives, and empty input
Say the brute force idea first, with its complexity
Name the pattern you plan to use and explain why it fits
Code cleanly, then test with a normal case and an edge case
State the final time and space complexity

sections.heading: Edge Cases Checklist
items: Empty input or a single element
All elements equal
Negative numbers and zeros
Duplicates
Very large values (use Long to avoid overflow)
Already sorted or reverse sorted input
Disconnected graphs and cycles
Null root in trees

sections.heading: Key Takeaways
items: Identify the input type, goal and constraints before coding
Constraints tell you the target complexity
Keywords in the statement point to specific patterns
Always start with brute force and then optimize
Many problems combine two patterns, such as Binary Search + Greedy
Practice naming the pattern before writing any code
